title: Stealing Harvard
full_review:
A young man enlists his witless pal to help him get $30,000 to fund his niece's college tuition in the silly comedy "Stealing Harvard" (Columbia).

Eager to marry his live-in love Elaine (Leslie Mann), John (Jason Lee) is delighted to find they have saved their goal of a $30,000 down payment for a house and so now can set the date.

Unexpectedly, however, John's niece, Noreen (Tammy Blanchard), has beaten the odds and been accepted at Harvard University. She and her single mom (Megan Mullally) remind John of his long-forgotten promise, caught on videotape, that if Noreen studied hard and got into college he would pay the bills. Thirty thousand is just the amount she needs and John hasn't got the heart to say no -- or to tell his fiancee to forget her dream house.Turning to his buddy Duff (Tom Green), he reluctantly agrees to what becomes several harebrained schemes to steal the money. They naturally go awry, and adding to John's problems is that his boss and future father-in-law (Dennis Farina) is determined to see that John never weds his precious daughter. Also skulking around is a police detective (John C. McGilney) who has John in his sights as the prime suspect in the bungled attempted robberies.

As directed by Bruce McColloch, the film's dopey characters and absurd situations are only a tad amusing. But happily, the gross-out humor usually present in a Tom Green flick doesn't materialize and he plays second fiddle to Lee, whose character has a certain amount of goofy charm.

In the humorous treatment of theft the characters seem to feel bad about stealing until they realize the insurance companies will foot the bill, which certainly is a wrongheaded rationalization, but nothing is meant to be taken too seriously in this inane comedy.

With nothing outstanding about this failed caper flick it's likely to disappear from the box office rather quickly, which is no loss to movie lovers.

Because of comic treatment of crime, a live-in relationship with discreet sexual situations, fleeting violence, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
